verses.verse:
युक्ताहार विहाराभ्याम ब्रम्हचारि व्रते स्थितः।
प्राण जिह्वांगुलीयांञ्च साधयेद् धैर्य पूर्वकम।६१।
verses.text: Through balanced āhāra and vihāra, and keeping to the vow of brahmacarya, one should patiently train the breath, the tongue and the fingers.

commentary.text: That is, delighting in the five objects taken in through the body's five organs of knowledge is called āhāra (intake), and the activities done through the five organs of action are called vihāra (conduct). To sift these two through far-sightedness and fine discernment and to keep the mind in control over them is itself a yoga. Practice of the bānsurī too is not possible without yoga.

Along with this, to remove the natural restlessness of the mind, it will be necessary to look upon the various feelings towards many many-coloured things and persons, in the light of knowledge, with a sense of oneness. The essence of all things and persons seen in this way is called Brahman. One who moves the mind in That is called a brahmacārī. To take care of the body's subtle but precious element, that is to protect the vīrya (semen), is also a principal part of brahmacarya (continence, discipline). In common usage a one-sided form of brahmacarya is current; in the sādhanā (practice) of the bānsurī this is necessary.

So, by reforming āhāra and vihāra in this way, try to bring simplicity into life. Then, while keeping brahmacarya, one should practise the prāṇa (breath), jihvā (tongue) and fingers by the methods below. Bear in mind that with a feeling of śraddhā (reverence) sādhanā becomes easy, whereas with a feeling of envy sādhanā becomes harsh. A feeling of hatred or envy towards any person, or of greed for any thing or position, arises of itself. To regard these as destroyers of the yajña (sacrifice) of sādhanā and to disregard them, and to keep setting up again and again in the mind the feeling of reverence towards knowledge, is the sādhaka's mental yajña.
